title: The North Face 2-Meter Dome review: an expedition basecamp you can stand up in
dek: A 4-season, eight-person geodesic dome built on twelve 11 mm Easton poles. It's a room, a kitchen and a storm shelter in one, and it weighs about 50 pounds.
subject: The North Face 2-Meter Dome
verdict: The 2-Meter Dome is a true expedition basecamp: huge, stand-up headroom, heavy fabrics and a twelve-pole geodesic frame. Owners treat it as a living room for weeks at a time. It's far too heavy to carry, and the roof vent design frustrates some owners, so it only makes sense for vehicle-supported or stationary camps.
bestFor: Expedition and research basecamps, long stays in one spot, group cooking and gathering space in cold or stormy places.
notFor: Anything you carry on your back, quick overnight trips, or campers who don't want a two-person, manual-in-hand setup.
pros: About 167 sq ft of floor with full standing height
Twelve 11 mm Easton 7075-E9 aluminum poles in a geodesic frame
Chimney vent, two windows and two doors
Owners report it handles a reasonable snow load
cons: Around 50 lb, so it lives in a truck or a basecamp
Setup is slow and confusing without the manual, and needs two people
Roof vent design lets water pool or bugs in, depending on how it's propped
body:
## The short version

The 2-Meter Dome replaced The North Face Dome 8 as the brand's biggest expedition tent. It's a four-season geodesic dome that sleeps eight, with about 167 square feet of floor and enough height that owners describe standing fully upright inside. One professional climber reviewing it on Trailspace used it for two months as his living room, bedroom, kitchen and art studio.

That tells you who it's for. This is basecamp infrastructure, not a tent you pitch for a night and pack the next morning.

## Space and layout

Owners consistently call it roomy, with one describing it as basically a full-sized room. Two zippered doors, two exterior windows, a chimney vent and interior canopy loops make it practical for long stays. There's even a stove hole in the floor for a properly vented basecamp stove setup.

## Strength and weather

The frame is twelve 11 mm Easton 7075-E9 aluminum poles crossing in a geodesic pattern, which spreads wind and snow load across many intersections. Owners say it tolerates a reasonable snow load, and they describe the fabrics as heavy-duty, with one comparing the 420-denier floor to backpack-grade Cordura.

The common complaint is the roof vent. Without its aluminum prop pole, water can pool on the fly. With the pole in, the top screen stays open and lets bugs in. One owner called it a major oversight.

## Setup

Expect a learning curve. One owner who had pitched it before had it up in under 30 minutes. Another said one-person setup is impossible, two-person setup is difficult, and the pole sequence isn't intuitive, so keep the manual with the tent. Practice at home before you need it in weather.

## Weight

At roughly 50 pounds it's vehicle-supported or helicopter-supported gear. Plan on carrying it in more than one load if there's any walk from the truck.

## Poles and parts

The 2-Meter Dome uses **12 poles**, **11 mm** tubing, **Easton 7075-E9 aluminum**.

Because the poles all cross each other, a single bent or snapped pole changes the shape of the whole dome. Replace a damaged pole rather than splinting it for long stays.

The North Face doesn't publish pole lengths. To match a replacement, lay your pole out straight, measure tip to tip, count the sections, and read the diameter printed near a joint (or use calipers). Then search the 2-Meter Dome in our [pole and parts finder](/poles?model=2-Meter%20Dome), compare against measured stock in the [pole size chart](/poles/sizes), or search by measurement in [find a pole by size](/poles/size).

## Bottom line

If you need a durable, stand-up group shelter for weeks in cold or stormy places, the 2-Meter Dome is one of the most serious tents ever sold for that job. For anything shorter or lighter, it's overkill.
